text:
ERISA Regulation - The Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (“ERISA”), provides for comprehensive federal regulation of certain employee
pension and benefit plans, including private employer and union sponsored health plans and certain other plans that contract with us to provide PBM services.
In general, the Company assists plan sponsors in the
25administration of their health benefit plans, including the prescription drug benefit portion of those plans, in accordance with the plan designs adopted by the
plan sponsors. In addition, the Company may have fiduciary duties where it has specifically contracted with a plan sponsor to accept limited fiduciary
responsibility, such as for the adjudication of initial prescription drug benefit claims and/or the appeals of denied claims under a plan. In addition to its
fiduciary provisions, ERISA imposes civil and criminal liability on service providers to health plans and certain other persons if certain forms of illegal
remuneration are made or received. These provisions of ERISA are broadly written and their application to specific business practices is often uncertain.
Some of the Company’s health and related benefits and large case pensions products and services and related fees also are subject to potential issues raised by
judicial interpretations relating to ERISA. Under those interpretations, together with DOL regulations, the Company may have ERISA fiduciary duties with
respect to medical members, PBM members and/or certain general account assets held under contracts that are not guaranteed benefit policies. As a result,
certain transactions related to those general account assets are subject to conflict of interest and other restrictions, and the Company must provide certain
disclosures to policyholders annually. The Company must comply with these restrictions or face substantial penalties.

title: Preemption
heading: 10.3.19 Preemption
start_phrase: ERISA generally preempts all state and local laws that relate to employee benefit plans, but the extent of the preemption continues to be reviewed by courts, including the U.S. Supreme Court.
summary: The excerpt outlines the Company’s regulatory and legal exposure under ERISA and evolving federal/state initiatives that could materially affect its health benefits and PBM operations. It explains that the Company may assume limited ERISA fiduciary duties by contract (e.g., claims adjudication and appeals) and faces civil/criminal liability for prohibited remuneration. Judicial interpretations and DOL regulations may impose fiduciary obligations for medical and PBM members and for certain general account assets, triggering conflict-of-interest restrictions and annual disclosure requirements, with substantial penalties for non-compliance. The section reviews ERISA preemption and recent court decisions (including U.S. Supreme Court and appellate rulings) that uphold various state PBM regulations, note continuing challenges to ERISA and Medicare Part D preemption, and signal shifting boundaries between state regulation and federal preemption. It also highlights broad legislative and regulatory initiatives—domestic and international—that could impact revenues, medical benefit ratios, and operating results, including ongoing federal budget sequestration affecting Medicare payments (extended to 2030), uncertainty around future Medicare/Medicaid funding and entitlement reforms, GDPR compliance in the EU, potential increases to the corporate tax rate, and multiple measures targeting PBM and pharmacy benefit design (e.g., eliminating manufacturer rebates, banning spread pricing, restricting formularies and tiering, limiting mail/specialty pharmacy requirements, curbing formulary/clinical program changes, and favoring upfront drug price discounts over rebates).
text:
Preemption - ERISA generally preempts all state and local laws that relate to employee benefit plans, but the extent of the preemption continues to be
reviewed by courts, including the U.S. Supreme Court. For example, in December 2020, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld an Arkansas law that, among other
things, mandates a particular pricing methodology, establishes an appeals process for a pharmacy when the reimbursement is below the pharmacy’s acquisition
cost, permits a pharmacy to reverse and rebill if they cannot procure the drug from its wholesaler at a price equal to or less than the reimbursement rate,
prohibits a PBM from reimbursing a pharmacy less than the amount it reimburses an affiliate on a per unit basis, and permits a pharmacy to decline to dispense
if the reimbursement is lower than the pharmacy’s acquisition cost. Subsequently, in November 2021, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit upheld a
North Dakota law that regulates employer-sponsored ERISA health plans and certain PBM practices within Medicare and in April 2022 the U.S. District Court
for the Western District of Oklahoma affirmed that the Oklahoma Insurance Department could enforce a state law against PBMs that contained provisions that
alter and limit some of the options that an ERISA plan can use, because none of the provisions mandate that ERISA plans make any specific choices.
Additional litigation has been filed in several states to challenge ERISA and Medicare Part D preemption.

title: Other Legislative Initiatives and Regulatory Initiatives
heading: 10.3.20 Other Legislative Initiatives and Regulatory Initiatives

text:
Other Legislative Initiatives and Regulatory Initiatives - The U.S. federal and state governments, as well as governments in other countries where the
Company does business, continue to enact and seriously consider many broad-based legislative and regulatory proposals that have had a material impact on or
could materially impact various aspects of the health care and related benefits system and the Company’s businesses, operating results and/or cash flows. For
example:
•Under the Budget Control Act of 2011 and the American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012 significant, automatic across-the-board budget cuts (known as
sequestration) began in March 2013, including Medicare spending cuts of not more than 2% of total program costs per year through 2024. Since then,
Congress has extended and modified the Medicare sequester a number of times. The CARES Act temporarily suspended the Medicare sequester and
extended mandatory sequestration to 2030. In July 2022, the 2% Medicare sequester resumed. Significant uncertainty remains as to whether and how the
U.S. Congress will proceed with actions that create additional federal revenue and/or with entitlement reform. The Company cannot predict future federal
Medicare or federal or state Medicaid funding levels or the impact that future federal or state budget actions or entitlement program reform, if it occurs,
will have on the Company’s businesses, operations or operating results, but the effects could be materially adverse, particularly on the Company’s
Medicare and/or Medicaid revenues, MBRs and operating results.
•The European Union’s (“EU’s”) General Data Protection Regulation (“GDPR”) began to apply across the EU during 2018.
•Other significant legislative and/or regulatory measures which are or recently have been under consideration include the following:
•Increasing the corporate tax rate.
•Eliminating payment of manufacturer’s rebates on prescription drugs to PBMs, PDPs and Managed Medicaid organizations in connection with
federally funded health care programs.
•Imposing requirements and restrictions on the design and/or administration of pharmacy benefit plans offered by the Company’s and its clients’
health plans and/or its PBM clients and/or the services the Company provides to those clients, including prohibiting “differential” or “spread”
pricing in PBM contracts; restricting or eliminating the use of formularies for prescription drugs; restricting the Company’s ability to require
members to obtain drugs through a home delivery or specialty pharmacy; restricting the Company’s ability to place certain specialty or other
drugs in the higher cost tiers of its pharmacy formularies; restricting the Company’s ability to make changes to drug formularies and/or clinical
programs; limiting or eliminating rebates on pharmaceuticals; requiring the use of up front purchase price discounts on pharmaceuticals in lieu of
rebates; restricting the Company’s ability to
26configure and reimburse its health plan and retail pharmacy provider networks, including use of CVS pharmacy locations; and restricting or
eliminating the use of certain drug pricing methodologies.
•Increasing federal or state government regulation of, or involvement in, the pricing and/or purchasing of drugs.
•Restricting the Company’s ability to limit providers’ participation in its networks and/or remove providers from its networks by imposing network
adequacy requirements or otherwise (including in its Medicare and Commercial Health Care Benefits products).
•Imposing assessments on (or to be collected by) health plans or health carriers that may or may not be passed through to their customers. These
assessments may include assessments for insolvency, the uninsured, uncompensated care, Medicaid funding or defraying health care provider
medical malpractice insurance costs.
•Mandating coverage by the Company’s and its clients’ health plans for additional conditions and/or specified procedures, drugs or devices (e.g.,
high cost pharmaceuticals, experimental pharmaceuticals and oral chemotherapy regimens).
•Regulating electronic connectivity.
•Mandating or regulating the disclosure of provider fee schedules, manufacturer’s rebates and other data about the Company’s payments to
providers and/or payments the Company receives from pharmaceutical manufacturers.
•Mandating or regulating disclosure of provider outcome and/or efficiency information.
•Prescribing or limiting members’ financial responsibility for health care or other covered services they utilize, including restricting “surprise” bills
by providers and by specifying procedures for resolving “surprise” bills.
•Prescribing payment levels for health care and other covered services rendered to the Company’s members by providers who do not have
contracts with the Company.
•Assessing the medical device status of home infusion therapy products and/or solutions, mobile consumer wellness tools and clinical decision
support tools, which may require compliance with FDA requirements in relation to some of these products, solutions and/or tools.
•Restricting the ability of employers and/or health plans to establish or impose member financial responsibility.
•Proposals to expand benefits under Original Medicare.
•Amending or supplementing ERISA to impose greater requirements on PBMs or the administration of employer-funded benefit plans or limit the
scope of current ERISA pre-emption, which would among other things expose the Company and other health plans to expanded liability for
punitive and other extra-contractual damages and additional state regulation.
It is uncertain whether the Company can counter the potential adverse effects of such potential legislation or regulation on its operating results or cash flows,
including whether it can recoup, through higher premium rates, expanded membership or other measures, the increased costs of mandated coverage or benefits,
assessments, fees, taxes or other increased costs, including the cost of modifying its systems to implement any enacted legislation or regulations.
The Company’s businesses also may be affected by other legislation and regulations. The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act creates
incentives for whistleblowers to speak directly to the government rather than utilizing internal compliance programs and reduces the burden of proof under the
Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977 (the “FCPA”). There also are laws and regulations that set standards for the escheatment of funds to states.
Health savings accounts, health reimbursement arrangements and flexible spending accounts and certain of the tax, fee and subsidy provisions of the ACA also
are regulated by the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the IRS.
The Company also may be adversely affected by court and regulatory decisions that expand or revise the interpretations of existing statutes and regulations or
impose medical malpractice or bad faith liability. Federal and state courts, including the U.S. Supreme Court, continue to consider cases, and federal and state
regulators continue to issue regulations and interpretations, addressing bad faith liability for denial of medical claims, the scope of ERISA’s fiduciary duty
requirements, the scope of the False Claims Act and the pre-emptive effect of ERISA and Medicare Part D on state laws.

title: Contract Audits
heading: 10.3.21 Contract Audits
start_phrase: The Company is subject to audits of many of its contracts, including its PBM client contracts, its PBM rebate contracts, its PBM network contracts, its contracts relating to Medicare Advantage and/or Medicare Part D, the agreements the Company’s pharmacies enter into with other payors, its Medicaid contracts and its customer contracts.
summary:
- Broad regulatory and legislative risks for a diversified health insurer/PBM/retail pharmacy, including:
  - Limits or changes to drug pricing methodologies and greater federal/state involvement in drug pricing and purchasing.
  - Network regulations restricting the ability to manage provider participation and remove providers, including adequacy standards across Medicare and commercial products.
  - Mandated benefits and coverage expansions (e.g., high-cost/experimental drugs, oral chemo), and regulations on electronic connectivity.
  - Transparency mandates for provider fee schedules, manufacturer rebates, and provider outcomes/efficiency data.
  - Member cost-sharing restrictions, surprise-billing curbs and dispute resolution processes, and prescribed payments for out-of-network care.
  - Assessments on health plans/carriers (e.g., insolvency, uninsured, uncompensated care, Medicaid support, malpractice costs).
  - Device status determinations for home infusion, wellness tools, and clinical decision support, potentially triggering FDA compliance.
  - Restrictions on employer/plan design of member financial responsibility and proposals to expand Original Medicare benefits.
  - Potential ERISA amendments expanding PBM/plan administration requirements and narrowing ERISA preemption, increasing exposure to state regulation and extra-contractual liabilities.

- Financial and operational impact uncertainty, including ability to offset mandated costs (benefits, fees, taxes, system changes) through premiums, membership growth, or other measures.

- Additional legal/regulatory frameworks affecting operations:
  - Dodd-Frank incentives for whistleblowers and changes impacting FCPA enforcement; state escheatment laws.
  - Treasury/IRS oversight of HSAs, HRAs, FSAs, and certain ACA tax/fee/subsidy elements.
  - Evolving court and regulatory interpretations on bad faith liability, ERISA fiduciary duties, False Claims Act scope, and ERISA/Medicare Part D preemption.

- Extensive contract audit exposure across PBM client, rebate, and network agreements; Medicare Advantage/Part D; Medicaid; and pharmacy payor contracts, including audits by federal and state agencies.

- Federal Employee Health Benefits (FEHB) program obligations:
  - OPM contracts with community rating, FEHB-specific MLR requirements alongside ACA MLR/rebates, and “cost-plus” arrangements implicating FEHB Acquisition Regulations.
  - OPM audits of MLR, premiums, and cost allocations, with potential premium refunds or sanctions for non-compliance.

- Clinical and administrative licensure:
  - State regulation of medicine, pharmacy, nursing, and other clinical practices; licensure/scope-of-practice compliance for disease management and clinical services.
  - State licensure/registration for TPAs, PPOs, utilization review entities, and discount/cash card programs.

- International regulatory environment:
  - Operations subject to varied, often stricter requirements (anti-corruption, sanctions, privacy/data protection including GDPR, data localization, tax/tariffs, corporate governance, labor, IP, consumer protection, insurance-specific rules, dividend/repatriation limits, local ownership), with Brexit-readiness noted.
  - Heightened exposure to U.S. FCPA and the UK Bribery Act.

- Anti-corruption compliance:
  - Risks tied to interactions with government-employed health professionals, with severe penalties and coordinated cross-border enforcement under FCPA/UK Bribery Act.

- Anti-money laundering:
  - Certain business lines subject to Treasury AML regulations and operating under established AML policies.
text:
Contract Audits - The Company is subject to audits of many of its contracts, including its PBM client contracts, its PBM rebate contracts, its PBM network
contracts, its contracts relating to Medicare Advantage and/or Medicare Part D, the agreements the Company’s pharmacies enter into with other payors, its
Medicaid contracts and its customer contracts. Because some of the Company’s contracts are with state or federal governments or with entities contracted with

title: Federal Employee Health Benefits Program
heading: 10.3.22 Federal Employee Health Benefits Program
start_phrase: The Company’s subsidiaries contract with the Office of Personnel Management (the “OPM”) to provide managed health care services under the FEHB program in their service areas.
summary:
- Participation in U.S. government health programs, including Medicaid (fee-for-service and managed), Medicare Part D, and Medicare Advantage.
- Federal Employee Health Benefits (FEHB) Program: contracts with OPM to provide managed care; premium rating rules; compliance with FEHB-specific minimum medical loss ratio (MLR) alongside ACA MLR and rebate requirements; pharmacy services for the Government-wide Service Benefit Plan via carriers like BlueCross BlueShield; cost-plus FEHB arrangements subject to the FEHB Act and FEHB Acquisition Regulation; OPM audits with potential premium refunds or sanctions for non-compliance.
- Clinical services regulation: state oversight of the practice of medicine, pharmacy, and nursing; clinician licensing and scope-of-practice requirements; disease management program participation.
- State licensure/registration for administrative entities: requirements for PPOs, third-party administrators, utilization review organizations, and consumer discount/cash card program administrators.
- International operations and regulation: global insurance licensing; post-Brexit measures to continue serving the EEA; exposure to diverse and often stricter laws on privacy/data protection (including GDPR), sanctions, insurance, tax, trade, corporate governance, labor, IP, consumer protection, reinsurance cessions, data/funds localization, dividend and capital repatriation limits, ownership localization, and higher taxes.
- Anti-corruption compliance: applicability of the U.S. FCPA and the UK Bribery Act (broader than FCPA), particularly given interactions with government-employed healthcare professionals; heightened SEC/DOJ enforcement and multi-jurisdictional penalty risk.

text:
Federal Employee Health Benefits Program - The Company’s subsidiaries contract with the Office of Personnel Management (the “OPM”) to provide
managed health care services under the FEHB program in their service areas. These contracts with the OPM and applicable government regulations establish
premium rating arrangements for this program. In addition to other requirements, such as the Transparency in Coverage Rule note above, OPM regulations
require that community-rated FEHB plans meet a FEHB program-specific minimum MLR by plan code and market. Managing to these rules is complicated by
the simultaneous application of the minimum MLR standards and associated premium rebate requirements of the ACA. The Company also has a contractual
arrangement with carriers for the FEHB program, such as the BlueCross BlueShield Association, to provide pharmacy services to federal employees, postal
workers, annuitants, and their dependents under the Government-wide Service Benefit Plan, as authorized by the FEHB Act and as part of the FEHB program.
Additionally, the Company manages certain FEHB plans on a “cost-plus” basis. These arrangements subject the Company to certain aspects of the FEHB Act,
and other federal regulations, such as the FEHB Acquisition Regulation, that otherwise would not be applicable to the Company. The OPM also is auditing the
Company and its other contractors to, among other things, verify that plans meet their applicable FEHB program-specific MLR and the premiums established
under the OPM’s Insured contracts and costs allocated pursuant to the OPM’s cost-based contracts are in compliance with the requirements of the applicable
FEHB program. The OPM may seek premium refunds or institute other sanctions against the Company if it fails to comply with the FEHB program
requirements.

title: Clinical Services Regulation
heading: 10.3.23 Clinical Services Regulation
start_phrase: The Company provides clinical services to health plans, PBMs and providers for a variety of complex and common medical conditions, including arranging for certain members to participate in disease management programs.
summary:
- Participation in U.S. government health programs, including Medicaid fee-for-service and managed Medicaid, Medicare Part D, and Medicare Advantage, with associated compliance obligations.
- Federal Employee Health Benefits (FEHB) program operations via OPM contracts: community rating and FEHB-specific minimum MLR requirements by plan code/market; complexities with concurrent ACA MLR and rebate rules; pharmacy services provided under the BCBS Government-wide Service Benefit Plan; some plans managed on a cost-plus basis subject to FEHB Act and Acquisition Regulation; OPM audits of MLR, premiums, and cost allocations with potential premium refunds or sanctions for noncompliance.
- Regulation of clinical services: state licensing and scope-of-practice requirements for physicians, pharmacists, nurses, and other clinicians; oversight of disease management programs.
- State licensure and registration for administrative entities: PPOs, TPAs, utilization review companies, and consumer/discount card program administrators.
- International regulatory environment: operations across multiple jurisdictions (including post-Brexit arrangements) subject to varied and sometimes stricter rules on anti-corruption, sanctions, privacy and data protection (GDPR), data transfer/mining, insurance, tax/tariff/trade, corporate governance, labor/employment, IP, consumer protection, investment, reinsurance cessions, localization of records/funds, higher taxes, dividend/repatriation limits, and local ownership requirements.
- Anti-corruption compliance: exposure to FCPA and UK Bribery Act due to interactions with government-employed healthcare professionals; heightened SEC/DOJ enforcement and potential multi-jurisdiction penalties.
- Anti-money laundering: certain business lines subject to U.S. Treasury AML regulations with implementing policies and controls.
text:
Clinical Services Regulation - The Company provides clinical services to health plans, PBMs and providers for a variety of complex and common medical
conditions, including arranging for certain members to participate in disease management programs. State laws regulate the practice of medicine, the practice
of pharmacy, the practice of nursing and certain other clinical activities. Clinicians engaged in a professional practice in connection with the provision of
clinical services must satisfy applicable state licensing requirements and must act within their scope of practice.

title: Third Party Administration and Other State Licensure Laws
heading: 10.3.24 Third Party Administration and Other State Licensure Laws
start_phrase: Many states have licensure or registration laws governing certain types of administrative organizations, such as PPOs, TPAs and companies that provide utilization review services.
summary:
- Participation in and regulation of government-sponsored health programs, including Medicaid (fee-for-service and managed care), Medicare Part D, and Medicare Advantage.
- Extensive involvement in the Federal Employees Health Benefits (FEHB) Program via OPM contracts, including:
  - Community rating and FEHB-specific minimum medical loss ratio (MLR) requirements by plan code and market.
  - Overlap and complexity with ACA minimum MLR and rebate rules.
  - Pharmacy services provided under the Government-wide Service Benefit Plan (e.g., via BlueCross BlueShield Association).
  - Cost-plus FEHB arrangements subject to the FEHB Act and FEHB Acquisition Regulation.
  - OPM audits of MLR compliance and premium/cost allocations, with potential refunds or sanctions for non-compliance.
- Regulation of clinical services, requiring state licensure and compliance with scope-of-practice rules for medicine, pharmacy, nursing, and related activities, including disease management programs.
- State licensure/registration for administrative functions, including PPOs, third-party administrators (TPAs), utilization review entities, and consumer discount/cash card programs.
- International regulatory landscape:
  - Operations and insurance licensing across multiple jurisdictions, with post-Brexit measures to continue serving the EEA.
  - Compliance with diverse and sometimes stricter laws on anti-corruption, economic sanctions, privacy/data protection (including GDPR), insurance, tax, tariffs/trade, corporate governance, data localization, labor/employment, IP, consumer protection, investment, local ownership/participation, reinsurance cessions, dividend/repatriation limits, and higher taxes.
  - Heightened exposure to U.S. and foreign anti-bribery/anti-corruption regimes (e.g., FCPA, UK Bribery Act).
- Anti-corruption compliance:
  - Prohibitions on offering value to foreign officials to obtain/retain business; applicability to interactions with government-employed healthcare professionals.
  - Significant SEC/DOJ enforcement and potential multi-jurisdictional penalties.
- Anti-money laundering compliance:
  - Certain business lines subject to U.S. Treasury AML regulations and implementation of AML policies.
text:
Third Party Administration and Other State Licensure Laws - Many states have licensure or registration laws governing certain types of administrative
organizations, such as PPOs, TPAs and companies that provide utilization review services. Several states also have licensure or registration laws governing the
organizations that provide or administer consumer card programs (also known as cash card or discount card programs).

title: International Regulation
heading: 10.3.25 International Regulation
start_phrase: The Company has insurance licenses in several foreign jurisdictions and does business directly or through local affiliations in numerous countries around the world.

It details participation in government health programs (Medicaid FFS and managed plans, Medicare Part D and Advantage, and FEHB), emphasizing FEHB-specific requirements: OPM contracts, community rating, program-specific minimum MLRs, interaction with ACA rebate rules, pharmacy services provided under the Government-wide Service Benefit Plan, “cost-plus” FEHB arrangements subject to the FEHB Act and Acquisition Regulation, and OPM audits with potential refunds or sanctions. It covers clinical services oversight, noting state licensure and scope-of-practice rules for clinicians; state licensure/registration for TPAs, PPOs, utilization review entities, and discount card program administrators; and international operations subject to diverse, often stricter requirements, including GDPR, sanctions, anti-corruption, data protection/transfer, employment, IP, tax, reinsurance cessions, localization, dividend/repatriation limits, and local ownership. The text highlights heightened exposure to and enforcement of anti-corruption laws (FCPA and the broader UK Bribery Act) due to interactions with government-employed healthcare professionals, and notes Treasury anti–money laundering regulations applicable to certain business lines with corresponding internal AML policies.
text:
International Regulation - The Company has insurance licenses in several foreign jurisdictions and does business directly or through local affiliations in
numerous countries around the world. The Company has taken steps to be able to continue to serve customers in the European Economic Area following the
United Kingdom’s exit from the EU (“Brexit”).
The Company’s international operations are subject to different, and sometimes more stringent, legal and regulatory requirements, which vary widely by
jurisdiction, including anti-corruption laws; economic sanctions laws; various privacy, insurance, tax, tariff and trade laws and regulations; corporate
governance, privacy, data protection (including the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation which began to apply across the EU during 2018), data mining,
data transfer, labor and employment, intellectual property, consumer protection and investment laws and regulations; discriminatory licensing procedures;
compulsory cessions of reinsurance; required localization of records and funds; higher premium and income taxes; limitations on dividends and repatriation of
capital; and requirements for local participation in an insurer’s ownership. In addition, the presence of operations in foreign countries potentially increases the
Company’s exposure to the anti-bribery, anti-corruption and anti-money laundering provisions of U.S. law, including the FCPA, and corresponding foreign
laws, including the U.K. Bribery Act 2010 (the “UK Bribery Act”).

title: Anti-Corruption Laws
heading: 10.3.26 Anti-Corruption Laws
start_phrase: The FCPA prohibits offering, promising or authorizing others to give anything of value to a foreign government official to obtain or retain business or otherwise secure a business advantage.
summary:
- Participation in U.S. government health programs, including Medicaid fee-for-service, Managed Medicaid, Medicare Part D, and Medicare Advantage.
- Federal Employee Health Benefits (FEHB) program operations: contracts with OPM; community rating and FEHB-specific minimum MLR requirements; interaction with ACA MLR rules; provision of pharmacy services (e.g., via BlueCross BlueShield Association); cost-plus FEHB arrangements subject to FEHB Act and FEHB Acquisition Regulation; ongoing OPM audits with potential premium refunds or sanctions for noncompliance.
- Clinical services regulation: state licensing and scope-of-practice requirements for clinicians (medicine, pharmacy, nursing) involved in disease management and other clinical services.
- Third-party administration and other state licensure: state laws governing PPOs, TPAs, utilization review entities, and administrators of consumer/discount card programs.
- International operations and compliance: insurance licensing abroad; post-Brexit continuity measures; exposure to varied and often stricter foreign laws covering anti-corruption, sanctions, privacy/data protection (including GDPR), insurance, tax, trade, corporate governance, labor, IP, consumer protection, investment; requirements such as reinsurance cessions, data/funds localization, higher taxes, dividend/repatriation limits, and local ownership participation.
- Anti-corruption compliance: applicability of the FCPA and the UK Bribery Act, particularly due to interactions with government-employed healthcare professionals; heightened enforcement risk and potential multi-jurisdictional penalties.
- Anti-money laundering (AML): certain business lines subject to U.S. Treasury AML rules and adoption of AML policies to ensure compliance.
text:
Anti-Corruption Laws - The FCPA prohibits offering, promising or authorizing others to give anything of value to a foreign government official to obtain or
retain business or otherwise secure a business advantage. The Company also is subject to applicable anti-corruption laws of the jurisdictions in which it
operates. In many countries outside the United States, health care professionals are employed by the government. Therefore, the Company’s dealings with them
are subject to regulation under the FCPA. Violations of the FCPA and other anti-corruption laws may result in severe criminal and civil sanctions as well as
other penalties, and there continues to be a heightened level of FCPA enforcement activity by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”) and
the DOJ. The UK Bribery Act is an anti-corruption law that is broader in scope than the FCPA and applies to all companies with a nexus to the United
Kingdom. Disclosures of FCPA violations may be shared with the UK authorities, thus potentially exposing companies to liability and potential penalties in
multiple jurisdictions.

title: Anti-Money Laundering Regulations
heading: 10.3.27 Anti-Money Laundering Regulations
start_phrase: Certain lines of the Company’s businesses are subject to Treasury anti-money laundering regulations.
summary:
- Participation in government-sponsored benefits programs, including Medicaid fee-for-service, Managed Medicaid, Medicare Part D, and Medicare Advantage, with associated regulatory obligations.
- Federal Employee Health Benefits (FEHB) program: contracts with OPM; FEHB-specific minimum medical loss ratio (MLR) requirements alongside ACA MLR and rebate rules; pharmacy services arrangements (e.g., with BlueCross BlueShield Association); cost-plus FEHB contracts subject to the FEHB Act and FEHB Acquisition Regulation; ongoing OPM audits and potential premium refunds or sanctions for noncompliance.
- Clinical services regulation: state licensure and scope-of-practice requirements for physicians, pharmacists, nurses, and other clinicians; oversight of disease management and related clinical programs.
- Third-party administration and other state licensure: state registration/licensure for PPOs, TPAs, utilization review entities, and consumer discount/cash card program administrators.
- International operations and regulation: insurance licensing in multiple foreign jurisdictions; post-Brexit measures to serve the EEA; broad exposure to diverse and sometimes stricter laws (anti-corruption, sanctions, privacy/data protection including GDPR, corporate governance, labor, IP, consumer protection, tax/tariff/trade); requirements such as reinsurance cessions, localization of records/funds, higher taxes, dividend/repatriation limits, and local ownership participation.
- Anti-corruption compliance: applicability of the U.S. FCPA and foreign laws (including the UK Bribery Act), particularly where health professionals are government employees; heightened SEC/DOJ enforcement and cross-border penalty exposure.
- Anti-money laundering: compliance with U.S. Treasury AML regulations and analogous non-U.S. AML laws.
- Sanctions compliance: subject to OFAC regulations and similar foreign sanctions regimes.
- FDA oversight: regulation of compounding pharmacy and clinical research; authority over medical devices (including a hemodialysis device in development and mobile medical devices) and retail pharmacy–sold products (prescription/OTC drugs, cosmetics, dietary supplements, certain foods); regulation of store-brand product distribution.
- Health Care Benefits segment–specific regulation: variability of state insurance rules hindering standardization; ACA and state requirements on premium rates, rating methodologies, underwriting, mandated benefits, sales/marketing, provider payment rates, network participation/removal limits, and financial solvency (reserves, risk-based capital); periodic reporting, examinations, license renewals, and dividend restrictions; additional licensure for PPO/MCO/utilization review/TPA activities; standards for service delivery, claims payment, fraud prevention, privacy/PHI protection, and coverage/payment practices.
- Required regulatory approvals and supervisory authority: need for approvals to price, market, and administer products; oversight by CMS, CCIIO, DOL, and state agencies with powers to grant/suspend/revoke licenses, exclude from government programs, limit marketing, regulate pricing/underwriting, assess fines/penalties, terminate or withhold payments under government contracts, impose retroactive premium adjustments and refunds, and restrict acquisitions or dispositions.
text:
Anti-Money Laundering Regulations - Certain lines of the Company’s businesses are subject to Treasury anti-money laundering regulations. Those lines of
business have implemented anti-money laundering policies designed to ensure their
28compliance with the regulations. The Company also is subject to anti-money laundering laws in non-U.S. jurisdictions where it operates.

title: Office of Foreign Assets Control
heading: 10.3.28 Office of Foreign Assets Control
start_phrase: The Company also is subject to regulation by the Office of Foreign Assets Control of the U.S. Department of Treasury (“OFAC”).
summary:
- The Company is subject to U.S. and international anti-money laundering requirements and sanctions laws, including oversight by the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), with comparable obligations in non-U.S. jurisdictions.
- The FDA regulates the Company’s compounding pharmacy and clinical research activities, as well as its involvement with medical devices (including a hemodialysis device and mobile medical devices) and a wide range of retail pharmacy products (prescription drugs, OTC medications, cosmetics, dietary supplements, certain food items). The Company is also regulated as a distributor of store-brand products.
- The Health Care Benefits segment faces extensive federal, state, local, and international regulation. Differing state insurance regimes and the ACA affect product standardization and impose constraints on premiums and rating, underwriting, mandated benefits, sales/marketing, provider payment rates, network participation and management, and financial solvency (reserves and risk-based capital).
- Health insurers and HMOs must file periodic reports, undergo examinations, and renew licenses; regulated subsidiaries face dividend restrictions. Various lines of business may require PPO, MCO, utilization review, or TPA licensure, with state-specific requirements covering networks, contracting, products/rates, financial standards, and reporting. Additional rules govern service delivery, claims payment, fraud prevention, protection of consumer health information, and payment for covered benefits.
- The Company must obtain and maintain approvals to price, market, and administer products. Supervisory bodies—including CMS, the Center for Consumer Information and Insurance Oversight, the DOL, and state agencies—can grant/suspend/revoke licenses; exclude the Company from government programs; limit marketing; regulate pricing and underwriting; levy damages, fines, and penalties; terminate contracts or withhold payments; impose retroactive premium adjustments and require refunds; and restrict mergers, acquisitions, or dispositions.
text:
Office of Foreign Assets Control - The Company also is subject to regulation by the Office of Foreign Assets Control of the U.S. Department of Treasury
(“OFAC”). OFAC administers and enforces economic and trade sanctions based on U.S. foreign policy and national security goals against targeted foreign
countries and regimes, terrorists, international narcotics traffickers, those engaged in activities related to the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and
other threats to the national security, foreign policy or economy of the United States. In addition, the Company is subject to similar regulations in the non-U.S.
jurisdictions in which it operates.

text:
Laws and Regulations Related to the Health Care Benefits Segment
In addition to the laws and regulations discussed above that may affect multiple segments of the Company’s business, the Company is subject to federal, state,
local and international statutes and regulations governing its Health Care Benefits segment specifically.

title: Overview
heading: 10.4.1 Overview
start_phrase: Differing approaches to state insurance regulation and varying enforcement philosophies may materially and adversely affect the Company’s ability to standardize its Health Care Benefits products and services across state lines.
summary:
- Describes the Company’s compliance obligations under U.S. and non-U.S. anti-money laundering laws and sanctions administered by the U.S. Treasury’s OFAC, as well as similar non-U.S. regimes.
- Explains FDA oversight of the Company’s compounding pharmacy and clinical research, and FDA authority over medical devices (including a hemodialysis device under development and mobile devices), prescription and OTC drugs, cosmetics, dietary supplements, certain foods, and the Company’s activities as a distributor of store-brand products.
- Outlines extensive regulation of the Health Care Benefits segment, noting state-by-state variability and ACA-driven requirements that affect product standardization, operations, and costs.
- Details key regulated areas: premium rates and methodologies, underwriting, mandated benefits, sales/marketing, provider payment rates, network participation limits, and financial solvency (reserves and risk-based capital).
- Notes ongoing reporting, examinations, and license renewals for insurers/HMOs; restrictions on subsidiary dividends; and state licensure requirements for PPO, MCO, utilization review, and TPA activities, including provider network, contracting, product/rate, financial, and reporting standards.
- Highlights legal standards for service delivery, claims payment, fraud prevention, consumer health information protection, and payment for covered services.
- Emphasizes the need for regulatory approvals to price, market, and administer products, and identifies oversight by CMS, CCIIO, DOL, and state health/insurance/Medicaid agencies.
- Summarizes broad regulatory enforcement powers: granting/suspending/revoking licenses; excluding from government programs; limiting marketing; regulating pricing/underwriting; imposing damages, fines, and penalties; terminating contracts or withholding payments; imposing retroactive premium adjustments and refunds; and restricting acquisitions or dispositions.
text:
Overview - Differing approaches to state insurance regulation and varying enforcement philosophies may materially and adversely affect the Company’s
ability to standardize its Health Care Benefits products and services across state lines. These laws and regulations, including the ACA, restrict how the
Company conducts its business and result in additional burdens and costs to the Company. Significant areas of governmental regulation include premium rates
and rating methodologies, underwriting rules and procedures, required benefits, sales and marketing activities, provider rates of payment, restrictions on health
plans’ ability to limit providers’ participation in their networks and/or remove providers from their networks and financial condition (including reserves and
minimum capital or risk based capital requirements). These laws and regulations are different in each jurisdiction and vary from product to product.
Each health insurer and HMO must file periodic financial and operating reports with the states in which it does business. In addition, health insurers and HMOs
are subject to state examination and periodic license renewal. Applicable laws also restrict the ability of the Company’s regulated subsidiaries to pay dividends,
and certain dividends require prior regulatory approval. In addition, some of the Company’s businesses and related activities may be subject to PPO, MCO,
utilization review or TPA-related licensure requirements and regulations. These licensure requirements and regulations differ from state to state, but may
contain provider network, contracting, product and rate, financial and reporting requirements. There also are laws and regulations that set specific standards for
the Company’s delivery of services, payment of claims, fraud prevention, protection of consumer health information, and payment for covered benefits and
services.

title: Required Regulatory Approvals
heading: 10.4.2 Required Regulatory Approvals
start_phrase: The Company must obtain and maintain regulatory approvals to price, market and administer many of its Health Care Benefits products.
summary:
- The company is subject to anti-money laundering laws outside the U.S. and to U.S. Treasury OFAC sanctions regulations, with comparable obligations in non-U.S. jurisdictions.
- The FDA regulates the company’s compounding pharmacy and clinical research, and oversees medical devices (including a hemodialysis device in development and mobile medical devices) and many pharmacy-sold products (prescription drugs, OTC medications, cosmetics, dietary supplements, certain foods). The company is also regulated as a distributor of store-brand products.
- Health Care Benefits segment oversight spans federal, state, local, and international rules that vary by jurisdiction and product, affecting premium rates and methodologies, underwriting, mandated benefits, marketing, provider payment rates, network participation and termination, and financial condition (reserves and risk-based capital).
- Regulated entities must file periodic reports, undergo examinations and license renewals, face restrictions on subsidiary dividends, and may require PPO/MCO/utilization review/TPA licenses with network, contracting, product, rate, financial, and reporting requirements. Additional laws govern service delivery, claims payment, fraud prevention, consumer health information protection, and benefit payments.
- Multiple agencies (CMS, CCIIO, DOL, and state health/insurance/Medicaid regulators) must approve pricing, marketing, and administration, and can license, suspend, or revoke operations; limit marketing; regulate pricing/underwriting; assess penalties; terminate or withhold government payments; mandate premium refunds or retroactive adjustments; restrict M&A; impose subsidiary capital and solvency requirements; regulate investments; and exclude plans from Public Exchanges for “unreasonable” rate increases. Operations are subject to routine and special audits, investigations, and information requests by various authorities.
- State laws restrict commercial pricing and underwriting (especially for small groups), limiting risk-based pricing and sometimes requiring disclosure of rating bases and restricting termination; they may also limit premium differentials between new and renewal business and across groups.
- The ACA expanded premium rate review for “reasonableness,” adding federal/state scrutiny and public disclosure, which can delay or constrain pricing and pressure medical benefit ratios and operating results during high utilization or unexpected cost trends.
- The ACA mandates minimum MLRs of 85% (large group) and 80% (individual/small group), with states able to impose stricter standards, higher floors, tighter definitions, prior rate approval, and other measures, limiting margins and exposing the company to fines, refunds, penalties, and litigation for noncompliance.
- The company has sought and expects to continue seeking significant commercial premium increases to address medical cost trends, coverage expansions, rating limits, and government assessments/fees/taxes, and to offset adverse selection, particularly in small groups; these requests carry risks of adverse publicity, regulatory pushback, denial/delay, and margin compression.
- In Medicaid and dual-eligible businesses targeted for growth, the company faces heightened exposure to policy and payment changes; states may adopt a minimum 85% MLR for Managed Medicaid plans, and must use reported MLR data in setting future rates.

title: Commercial Product Pricing and Underwriting Restrictions
heading: 10.4.3 Commercial Product Pricing and Underwriting Restrictions
start_phrase: Pricing and underwriting regulation by states limits the Company’s underwriting and rating practices and those of other health insurers, particularly for small employer groups, and varies by state.
summary:
- Regulatory oversight may require the company to maintain minimum capital in subsidiaries, monitor solvency and reserves, regulate investment quality/diversification, and potentially exclude plans from Public Exchanges for “unreasonable” premium increases or other HHS/state criteria.
- The company is subject to ongoing investigations, audits, examinations, and information requests from federal, state, and international regulators, including Attorneys General and legislators.
- State pricing and underwriting rules restrict how commercial premiums are set, especially for small groups, limiting risk-based pricing and the ability to reflect costs, and may cap differences between new and renewal rates, require disclosure of rating bases, and limit termination rights.
- The ACA expanded premium rate review with heightened state/federal scrutiny and public disclosure for increases at or above specified thresholds, potentially delaying or preventing adequate pricing and impacting medical cost margins and results.
- ACA minimum medical loss ratio (MLR) requirements (85% large group; 80% individual/small group) serve as floors; states can impose higher MLRs, stricter definitions, tie MLRs to prospective filings, and require prior approval, further compressing margins and exposing the company to refunds, fines, penalties, and litigation for noncompliance.
- The company has sought (for 2023) and expects to continue seeking significant commercial premium increases to address medical trend, mandated coverage expansions, rating limits, and federal/state assessments, fees, and taxes, as well as adverse selection—creating risks of denial/reduction/delay, adverse publicity/regulatory action, and operating margin compression.
- Medicaid expansion strategy (including dual eligible and special needs plans) increases exposure to policy and payment changes; federal rules allow states to set at least an 85% MLR for Managed Medicaid and require use of plan-reported MLR data in future rate setting.
text:
Commercial Product Pricing and Underwriting Restrictions - Pricing and underwriting regulation by states limits the Company’s underwriting and rating
practices and those of other health insurers, particularly for small employer groups, and varies by state. In general, these limitations apply to certain customer
segments and limit the Company’s ability to set prices for new or renewing groups, or both, based on specific characteristics of the group or the group’s prior
claim experience. In some states, these laws and regulations restrict the Company’s ability to price for the risk it assumes and/or reflect reasonable costs in the
Company’s pricing.
The ACA expanded the premium rate review process by, among other things, requiring the Company’s Commercial Insured rates to be reviewed for
“reasonableness” at either the state or the federal level. HHS established a federal premium rate review process that generally applies to proposed premium rate
increases equal to or exceeding a federally (or lower state) specified threshold. HHS’s rate review process imposes additional public disclosure requirements as
well as additional review on filings requesting premium rate increases equal to or exceeding this “reasonableness” threshold. These combined state and federal
review requirements may prevent, further delay or otherwise affect the Company’s ability to price for the risk it assumes, which could adversely affect its
MBRs and operating results, particularly during periods of increased utilization of medical services and/or medical cost trend or when such utilization and/or
trend exceeds the Company’s projections.
The ACA also specifies minimum MLRs of 85% for large group Commercial products and 80% for individual and small group Commercial products. Because
the ACA minimum MLRs are structured as “floors” for many of their requirements, states have the latitude to enact more stringent rules governing these
restrictions. For Commercial products, states have and may adopt higher minimum MLR requirements, use more stringent definitions of “medical loss ratio,”
incorporate minimum MLR requirements into prospective premium rate filings, require prior approval of premium rates or impose other requirements related
to minimum MLR. Minimum MLR requirements and similar actions further limit the level of margin the Company can earn in its Insured Commercial
products while leaving the Company exposed to medical costs that are higher than those reflected in its pricing. The Company also may be subject to
significant fines, penalties, premium refunds and litigation if it fails to comply with minimum MLR laws and regulations.
In addition, the Company requested increases in its premium rates in its Commercial Health Care Benefits business for 2023 and expects to request future
increases in those rates in order to adequately price for projected medical cost trends, required expansions of coverage and rating limits, and significant
assessments, fees and taxes imposed by the federal and state governments, including as a result of the ACA. The Company’s rates also must be adequate to
reflect adverse selection in its products, particularly in small group Commercial products. These rate increases may be significant and thus heighten the risks of
adverse publicity, adverse regulatory action and adverse selection and the likelihood that the Company’s requested premium rate increases will be denied,
reduced or delayed, which could lead to operating margin compression.
Many of the laws and regulations governing the Company’s pricing and underwriting practices also limit the differentials in premium rates insurers and other
carriers may charge between new and renewal business, and/or between groups based on differing characteristics. They may also require that carriers disclose
to customers the basis on which the carrier establishes new business and renewal premium rates and limit the ability of a carrier to terminate customers’
coverage.

title: Medicaid Regulation
heading: 10.4.4 Medicaid Regulation
start_phrase: The Company is seeking to substantially grow its Medicaid, dual eligible and dual eligible special needs plan businesses over the next several years.
summary:
- Regulatory oversight and potential sanctions: requirements to maintain minimum capital, monitor solvency and reserves; restrictions on investment quality/diversification; possible exclusion from Public Exchanges for unreasonable premium increases or failure to meet federal/state criteria.
- Investigations and audits: routine and special inquiries, audits, examinations, subpoenas, and information requests by federal, state, and international regulators, Attorneys General, and legislators.
- Commercial pricing and underwriting limits: state rules constrain rate setting and underwriting (especially for small groups), cap differentials between new/renewal business, mandate disclosure of rating bases, and limit termination rights.
- ACA rate review and transparency: expanded “reasonableness” reviews for premium increases above thresholds, added public disclosures, and potential delays/denials that can pressure MBRs and operating results.
- Minimum medical loss ratios (MLRs): ACA floors (85% large group; 80% individual/small group) with states able to impose stricter standards and definitions, integrate MLRs into prospective rate filings, and require prior approval; noncompliance risks include fines, refunds, penalties, and litigation.
- Premium rate actions and risks: planned and future rate increases to address medical cost trends, coverage expansions, rating limits, and government fees/taxes; heightened risks of adverse publicity, regulatory pushback, adverse selection, and margin compression.
- Medicaid and dual-eligible business exposure: planned growth increases sensitivity to policy and payment changes; states can set ≥85% MLRs for Managed Medicaid or use reported MLR data to calibrate rates; stricter definitions and network adequacy standards can further limit margins and increase risk.
- Evolving Medicaid landscape: varying state expansion status and potential reversals due to elections; 2020 managed care rule changes introducing flexibility in rate setting/network adequacy and new operational requirements (communications, appeals/grievances, provider directories).
- Program economics and contracting: state-by-state premium variability; potential reforms (e.g., drug rebate restrictions for MCOs/PBMs, expanded risk-based managed care, benefit/reimbursement/eligibility/network changes including mandated high-cost providers); contracts may be canceled on short notice or due to insufficient funding; some markets may be uneconomic.
- Compliance and enforcement in Medicaid/dual-eligible programs: extensive CMS and state oversight, audits, encounter data obligations, and complex, changing regulations requiring significant resources; potential sanctions include fines, payment withholds, refunds, contract terminations/non-renewals, marketing/enrollment suspensions, program exclusion, and civil monetary penalties.
- Federal and state reporting: broad financial/business reporting with penalties for inaccuracies/omissions; reliance on third-party data; ongoing system changes and resource commitments required, with residual risk of report errors or data unavailability.
text:
Medicaid Regulation - The Company is seeking to substantially grow its Medicaid, dual eligible and dual eligible special needs plan businesses over the next
several years. As a result, the Company also is increasing its exposure to changes in government policy with respect to and/or regulation of the various
Medicaid, dual eligible and dual eligible special needs plan programs in which the Company participates, including changes in the amounts payable to the
Company under those programs.
In addition to a quality rating system that applies to Medicaid and Managed Medicaid plans, federal regulations give states the option to choose to establish a
minimum MLR of at least 85% for their Managed Medicaid plans, including those offered by the Company. Regardless of whether a state establishes a
minimum MLR, it must use plan-reported MLR data to set future
30payment rates for managed care, so that its plans will “reasonably achieve” an MLR of at least 85%. For Managed Medicaid products, states may use more
stringent definitions of “medical loss ratio”, use discretion in choosing a quantitative standard for determining provider network adequacy, or impose other
requirements related to minimum MLR. Minimum MLR requirements and similar actions further limit the level of margin the Company can earn in its Insured
Medicaid products while leaving the Company exposed to medical costs that are higher than those reflected in its pricing. The Company also may be subject to
significant fines, penalties, premium refunds and litigation if it fails to comply with minimum MLR laws and regulations.
States continue to consider Medicaid expansion; however, to date 12 states have not expanded, which will drop to 11 states once South Dakota’s expansion
takes effect in July 2023. States may opt out of the elements of the ACA requiring expansion of Medicaid coverage without losing their current federal
Medicaid funding. In addition, the election of new Governors and/or state legislatures may impact states’ previous decisions regarding Medicaid expansion.
Although Congress enacted incentives for states that had not yet done so to expand Medicaid, this incentive alone may not persuade holdout states to expand.
In 2021, Medicaid MCOs faced new requirements and state flexibility that were finalized in the 2020 Medicaid managed care final rule. States now have
flexibility related to rate setting and provider network adequacy that could adversely or positively impact our Medicaid plans. Other changes related to
managed care operations include beneficiary communications, appeals and grievances, and provider directories.
The economic aspects of the Medicaid, dual eligible and dual eligible special needs plan business vary from state to state and are subject to frequent change.
Medicaid premiums are paid by each state and differ from state to state. The federal government and certain states also are considering proposals and
legislation for Medicaid and dual eligible program reforms or redesigns, including restrictions on the collection of manufacturer’s rebates on pharmaceuticals
by Medicaid MCOs and their contracted PBMs, further program, population and/or geographic expansions of risk-based managed care, increasing beneficiary
cost-sharing or payment levels, and changes to benefits, reimbursement, eligibility criteria, provider network adequacy requirements (including requiring the
inclusion of specified high cost providers in the Company’s networks) and program structure. In some states, current Medicaid and dual eligible funding and
premium revenue may not be adequate for the Company to continue program participation. The Company’s Medicaid and dual eligible contracts with states (or
sponsors of Medicaid managed care plans) are subject to cancellation by the state (or the sponsors of the managed care plans) after a short notice period
without cause (e.g., when a state discontinues a managed care program) or in the event of insufficient state funding.
The Company’s Medicaid, dual eligible and dual eligible special needs plan products also are heavily regulated by CMS and state Medicaid agencies, which
have the right to audit the Company’s performance to determine compliance with CMS contracts and regulations. The Company’s Medicaid products, dual
eligible products and CHIP contracts also are subject to complex federal and state regulations and oversight by state Medicaid agencies regarding the services
provided to Medicaid enrollees, payment for those services, network requirements (including mandatory inclusion of specified high-cost providers), and other
aspects of these programs, and by external review organizations which audit Medicaid plans on behalf of state Medicaid agencies. The laws, regulations and
contractual requirements applicable to the Company and other participants in Medicaid and dual eligible programs, including requirements that the Company
submit encounter data to the applicable state agency, are extensive, complex and subject to change. The Company has invested significant resources to comply
with these standards, and its Medicaid and dual eligible program compliance efforts will continue to require significant resources. CMS and/or state Medicaid
agencies may fine the Company, withhold payments to the Company, seek premium and other refunds, terminate the Company’s existing contracts, elect not to
award the Company new contracts or not to renew the Company’s existing contracts, prohibit the Company from continuing to market and/or enroll members
in or refuse to automatically assign members to one or more of the Company’s Medicaid or dual eligible products, exclude the Company from participating in
one or more Medicaid or dual eligible programs and/or institute other sanctions and/or civil monetary penalties against the Company if it fails to comply with
CMS or state regulations or contractual requirements.
The Company cannot predict whether pending or future federal or state legislation or court proceedings will change various aspects of the Medicaid program,
nor can it predict the impact those changes will have on its business operations or operating results, but the effects could be materially adverse.

title: Federal and State Reporting
heading: 10.4.5 Federal and State Reporting
start_phrase: The Company is subject to extensive financial and business reporting requirements, including penalties for inaccuracies and/or omissions, at both the federal and state level.
summary:
- Minimum medical loss ratio (MLR) requirements: States and CMS require managed care plans to target an MLR of at least 85%, limiting margins and exposing the Company to medical cost volatility. Noncompliance can trigger fines, penalties, premium refunds, and litigation.
- Medicaid expansion and political uncertainty: While most states have expanded Medicaid (South Dakota effective July 2023), several have not; gubernatorial and legislative changes and federal incentives create ongoing uncertainty about expansion decisions.
- 2020 Medicaid managed care final rule impacts: Greater state flexibility in rate setting and provider network adequacy may help or hurt plan performance; added operational requirements cover beneficiary communications, appeals and grievances, and provider directories.
- State-by-state variability and reform risks: Economic terms, premiums, and funding levels vary widely and change frequently. Potential reforms include limits on drug manufacturer rebate collection by MCOs/PBMs, broader risk-based managed care expansions, changes to cost-sharing, benefits, reimbursement, eligibility, and mandated inclusion of high-cost providers—any of which could pressure margins or participation viability.
- Contract fragility: Medicaid and dual eligible (including DSNP) contracts can be canceled on short notice without cause or due to insufficient state funding, threatening revenue continuity.
- Intensive regulation and oversight: CMS and state Medicaid agencies, plus external review organizations, conduct audits and enforce complex, evolving requirements (including encounter data submission and network rules). Noncompliance risks include payment withholds, refunds, marketing/enrollment freezes, contract termination or nonrenewal, exclusion from programs, sanctions, and civil monetary penalties.
- Legislative and judicial uncertainty: Future federal or state actions affecting Medicaid are unpredictable and could materially adversely impact operations and results.
- Extensive federal and state reporting: The Company faces rigorous reporting obligations with penalties for errors or omissions, relies on third-party data that may be incomplete or unreliable, and must invest substantially in systems and resources—yet cannot fully eliminate reporting error risks.
text:
Federal and State Reporting - The Company is subject to extensive financial and business reporting requirements, including penalties for inaccuracies and/or
omissions, at both the federal and state level. The Company’s ability to comply with certain of these requirements depends on receipt of information from third
parties that may not be readily available or reliably provided in all instances. The Company is and will continue to be required to modify its information
systems, dedicate significant resources and incur significant expenses to comply with these requirements. However, the Company cannot eliminate the risks of
unavailability of or errors in its reports.

title: Product Design and Administration and Sales Practices
heading: 10.4.6 Product Design and Administration and Sales Practices
start_phrase: State and/or federal regulatory scrutiny of health care benefit product design and administration and marketing and advertising practices, including the filing of insurance policy forms, the adequacy of provider networks, the accuracy of provider directories, and the adequacy of disclosure regarding products and their administration, is increasing as are the penalties being imposed for inappropriate practices.
summary:
- Heightened state and federal oversight of health care product design, administration, and sales/marketing, with emphasis on policy form filings, provider network adequacy, provider directory accuracy, and disclosure practices; penalties for noncompliance are increasing, with particular scrutiny on Medicare, Medicaid, dual-eligible, and limited-benefit products.
- Guaranty fund/solvency framework: insurers can be assessed to cover obligations of insolvent insurers, including long-term care and health insurers; assessments are typically based on relative premium volume by state. Some states allow recovery via premium tax offsets, but rising assessments could prompt limits on future offsets; similar regimes may apply to HMOs and other ACA-established payors.
- Expanding state regulation of PBM activities may impair the ability to operate on commercially reasonable terms and to standardize PBM offerings across states.
- Influence of quasi-regulatory bodies and credentialing organizations (e.g., NABP, NCOIL, URAC) through model regulations and standards that may shape state laws and client requirements, affecting PBM, mail order, specialty pharmacy operations, and health plan services.
- PBM activities are subject to federal and state laws, including the False Claims Act and anti-kickback statutes, which govern or may further restrict: manufacturer rebates and other payments; formulary management; MAC/AWP pricing and clinical programs; spread pricing and pricing reconciliations; third-party data disclosures; drug utilization management; PBM duties to clients; network configuration; pharmacy operations and audits; disclosure of provider reimbursement rates; and fees tied to administrative services and patient care; plus PBM registration/licensing. Noncompliance can lead to material fines, sanctions, and adverse operating/cash flow impacts.
- Although PBM service contracts are generally not regulated as insurance, state insurance departments are increasing oversight via licensure/registration, market conduct examinations, and audits, with active rulemaking on licensure, pharmacy reimbursement, network design, member cost sharing, and pharmacy audits.

Product Design and Administration and Sales Practices - State and/or federal regulatory scrutiny of health care benefit product design and administration

title: Guaranty Fund Assessments/Solvency Protection
heading: 10.4.7 Guaranty Fund Assessments/Solvency Protection
start_phrase: Under guaranty fund laws existing in all states, insurers doing business in those states can be assessed (in most states up to prescribed limits) for certain obligations of insolvent insurance companies to policyholders and claimants.
summary:
- Heightened regulatory scrutiny of health benefit product design, administration, marketing, and advertising, including policy form filings, provider network adequacy, provider directory accuracy, and product/disclosure adequacy; penalties are increasing. Special focus on Medicare, Medicaid, dual-eligible, and limited-benefit products.
- Guaranty fund assessments/solvency protection: States assess insurers to cover obligations of insolvent insurers (including long-term care and health). Assessments are based on state premium share; some recovery via premium tax offsets, though rising assessments could prompt limits on offsets. Similar regimes may apply to HMOs and other ACA-related payors.
- Expanding state and quasi-regulatory oversight of PBMs: Many states have enacted or proposed comprehensive PBM regulations, potentially hindering standardization and commercial terms across states. Organizations like NABP, NCOIL, and URAC influence state adoption and client requirements despite not having legal force.
- PBM activities face extensive federal and state regulation (e.g., False Claims Act, Anti-Kickback Statute and state analogues) governing rebate practices, formularies, MAC/AWP pricing, clinical programs, spread pricing, pricing guarantees, data disclosures, utilization management, network configuration, pharmacy operations/audits, reimbursement transparency, fee disclosures, and PBM registration/licensing. Noncompliance can lead to material fines, sanctions, and adverse financial effects.
- Although PBM service contracts typically are not insurance-regulated, state insurance departments increasingly oversee PBMs via licensure/registration, market conduct exams, and rulemaking on reimbursement, network design, cost sharing, and pharmacy audits.
text:
Guaranty Fund Assessments/Solvency Protection - Under guaranty fund laws existing in all states, insurers doing business in those states can be assessed (in
most states up to prescribed limits) for certain obligations of insolvent insurance companies to policyholders and claimants. The life and health insurance
guaranty associations in which the Company participates that operate under these laws respond to insolvencies of long-term care insurers as well as health
insurers. The Company’s assessments generally are based on a formula relating to the Company’s health care premiums in the state compared to the premiums
of other insurers. Certain states allow assessments to be recovered over time as offsets to premium taxes. Some states have similar laws relating to HMOs
and/or other payors such as not-for-profit consumer governed health plans established under the ACA. While historically the Company has ultimately
recovered more than half of guaranty fund assessments through statutorily permitted premium tax offsets, significant increases in assessments could lead to
legislative and/or regulatory actions that limit future offsets.

Laws and Regulations Related to the Pharmacy Services Segment
In addition to the laws and regulations discussed above that may affect multiple segments of the Company’s business, the Company is subject to federal, state
